t.5.13.1: Standing there, he gazed about, searching for Maithilī, and, looking down upon the earth, he surveyed all of it.
t.5.13.3: He beheld that grove, resembling Nandana, filled with beasts and birds, crowded with mansions and palaces, and resounding with the calls of cuckoos.
t.5.13.2: That grove was graced with saṃtānaka creepers and trees, endowed with heavenly fragrances and flavors, and richly adorned on every side.
t.5.13.4: It was adorned with ponds bright with golden water-lilies and lotuses, furnished with many seats and carpets, and filled with many underground chambers.
t.5.13.5: With its lovely trees bearing the flowers of every season and laden with fruit, and with the splendor of its blossoming aśoka trees, the grove shone with the radiance of the rising sun.
t.5.13.7: With aśoka trees, dispellers of sorrow, heaped with blossoms right down to their roots, and so heavily burdened by the weight of their flowers that they seemed to touch the earth.
t.5.13.6: Standing there, Māruti beheld it, seemingly ablaze, as though its branches were again and again being stripped of leaves by the birds swooping down in hundreds, many-hued and wearing flowers as crests.
t.5.13.8: With karṇikāra trees in blossom and kiṃśuka trees richly flowered, that place, by their radiance, seemed ablaze on every side.
t.5.13.9: Many punnāga and saptaparṇa trees, and likewise campaka and uddālaka trees, with well-grown roots and in full bloom, shone forth splendidly.
t.5.13.10: There were aśoka trees there by the thousands: some resembling refined gold, some like tongues of fire, and some like dark collyrium.
t.5.13.11: With its many kinds of gardens it was like Nandana, and it was as colourful as Caitraratha; it seemed to surpass even these, beyond imagining, divine, delightful, and wrapped in splendour.
t.5.13.13: That delightful garden was filled with trees bearing the flowers of every season and fragrant with the scent of honey, and with herds of deer and birds of many varied cries.
t.5.13.12: It was like a second sky, filled with hosts of flowers for stars, and, bright with hundreds of flowers for jewels, it was like a fifth ocean.
t.5.13.15: There in that aśoka grove, the bull among monkeys saw, standing not far off, a mighty sanctuary-palace.
t.5.13.14: It carried the flow of many fragrances, was sweet with holy scent and delightful to the mind, like a second Gandhamādana, that lord of mountains rich in fragrance.
t.5.13.16: In the midst he saw it standing upon a thousand pillars, white as Kailāsa, with stairways made of coral and platforms of refined gold.
t.5.13.18: Then he saw her, clad in soiled garments, surrounded by rākṣasīs, emaciated from fasting, wretched, sighing again and again, like the spotless crescent of the moon at the beginning of the bright fortnight.
t.5.13.17: It seemed to steal away the eyes and to blaze with splendor; spotless, and so lofty that it seemed to scrape the sky.
t.5.13.20: Clad in a single yellow garment, an excellent cloth now soiled, mud-stained and without ornaments, she was like a lotus pond bereft of its lotuses.
t.5.13.21: He saw her, abashed, scorched by sorrow, withered and pitiable, like Rohiṇī oppressed by the planet Aṅgāraka.
t.5.13.19: Her of lovely radiance, whose form showed only faintly, like the flame of fire wrapped in a net of smoke.
t.5.13.23: She saw no one dear to her, but only the throng of rākṣasīs, like a doe separated from her herd and surrounded by a pack of dogs.
t.5.13.22: Her face streaming with tears, forlorn, and wasted from fasting, she was wholly given over to grief and brooding, miserable, and forever sunk in sorrow.
t.5.13.24: Her single braid, like a dark serpent, fell to her hips; she who deserved happiness was scorched by sorrow, a stranger to misfortunes.
t.5.13.25: Seeing that large-eyed woman, exceedingly soiled and emaciated, he concluded, by reasons that pointed to it, that she was Sītā.
t.5.13.27: The goddess with a face like the full moon, with lovely brows and beautifully rounded breasts, who by her radiance was making all the quarters free of darkness.
t.5.13.26: Just as we saw her then, while she was being carried off by that rākṣasa who could take any form at will, so indeed does this lady appear now.
t.5.13.28: Her, Sītā, dark-haired, with lips like the bimba fruit, slender-waisted and finely formed, with eyes like lotus petals, like Rati, the beloved of Manmatha.
t.5.13.29: Her who was beloved of the whole world, like the radiance of the full moon, the fair-limbed lady seated on the ground like a self-restrained female ascetic.
t.5.13.30: Timid and sighing heavily, like the consort of a lord of serpents, she did not shine, being covered by a vast, wide-spread net of sorrow.
t.5.13.31: Her, like the flame of fire entangled in a web of smoke, like a memory clouded with doubt, like prosperity that has fallen into ruin.
t.5.13.32: He beheld her like faith that has been shattered, like hope that has been thwarted, like success beset with obstacles, like an understanding clouded with impurity.
t.5.13.33: She seemed like fame fallen low through a baseless slander, pained at being kept from Rāma and wasted away by her abduction at the hands of a rākṣasa.
t.5.13.34: The helpless woman, with eyes like a young fawn's, glancing about here and there, sighing again and again, her face cheerless and brimming with tears, the lashes of her eyes dark.
t.5.13.35: She bore a coating of dirt and mire, wretched, unadorned though worthy of adornment, like the radiance of the king of stars veiled by black clouds.
t.5.13.37: With difficulty did Hanumān recognize Sītā, bereft of ornaments, as one recognizes speech that, lacking proper refinement, has passed into another meaning.
t.5.13.36: But gazing at Sītā, his mind was seized with doubt again and again, as one doubts learning that has grown faint through neglect of reciting the sacred texts.
t.5.13.38: Beholding that wide-eyed, blameless princess, he reasoned that she was Sītā, establishing it by various signs.
t.5.13.39: He observed those many ornaments that graced her body, the very ones Rāma had once described as adorning the limbs of Vaidehī.
t.5.13.40: There were the well-made ear ornaments and the pair of dog-tooth-shaped pendants, firmly set in place, and on her hands the ornaments bright with gems and coral.
t.5.13.41: Darkened from being worn so long, yet still keeping their shape, these, I think, are the very ornaments that Rāma described.
t.5.13.42: Those ornaments that she let fall there I do not see on her; but those she did not cast off are these very ones, there is no doubt.
t.5.13.43: That lovely yellow garment, gleaming like a band of gold, the upper cloth that had slipped down and lay caught upon the mountain, was seen at that time by the monkeys.
t.5.13.44: And the excellent ornaments that were seen lying on the surface of the earth, large and jingling, were thrown down by this very woman.
t.5.13.45: Because it has been worn for so long, this garment is badly soiled and worn; yet surely its colour is just the same, as splendid as that of the other.
t.5.13.46: This woman with limbs the color of gold is the beloved queen of Rāma; though she is lost, she does not vanish from his mind.
t.5.13.47: This is she for whose sake Rāma is tormented by four things: by compassion, by tenderness, by grief, and by love.
t.5.13.48: Out of compassion, because she is a woman who is lost; out of kindness, because she depended on him; out of grief, because his wife is gone; and out of love, because she is his beloved.
t.5.13.49: Such is this lady's beauty, the grace of her every limb and feature, and such is the beauty of Rāma, that this dark-eyed one must be his.
t.5.13.50: The heart of this lady is fixed on him, and his heart is fixed on her; because of that, she and that righteous-souled one go on living even for a moment.
t.5.13.51: Mighty-armed Rāma does a thing most difficult to do, in that he lives even for a moment without this Sītā, a woman of intoxicating beauty.
t.5.13.52: Having thus seen Sītā then, the son of the Wind, overjoyed, went to Rāma in his mind and praised that lord.
